A seemingly natural alternative would be to form pairs
(human recording, TTS re-synthesis of the same text) and always treat the
human as the positive example. However, in preliminary experiments we found
that such supervision mainly trains a **deepfake detector** (“real vs
synthetic”), not a fine-grained naturalness judge *among synthetic outputs*.
Consistent with this, the existing deepfake detectors we include as baselines
in Table 2 perform **around chance** when asked to choose the more natural
sample between **two synthetic** audios, indicating that “real vs fake” cues
do not transfer well to our naturalness preference setting.

---

### (b) Mitigating model-bias inheritance: diversity and OOD tests

We agree that if a RM was trained only on data produced by a single TTS architecture, it
might simply latch onto that model’s artifacts (e.g., a particular vocoder
noise pattern). Thus, we aim to mitigate this when developing the SpeechJudge-GRM:

1. **Architectural and stylistic diversity in SpeechJudge-Data.**  
   We build the dataset from **multiple TTS families** (CosyVoice2,
   CosyVoice2-INTP, F5-TTS, MaskGCT, Ints-INTP, etc.) spanning:
   - different generation paradigms (autoregressive, flow-matching,
     masked generative models),
   - three linguistic regimes (Chinese, English, and Chinese–English
     code-switching),
   - and multiple styles (regular + expressive: emotional, accented, whisper,
     game).  
   This is intended to expose the judge to a **broad variety of artifacts**,
   rather than a single model’s idiosyncrasies.

2. **Evidence in the original submission: generalization to unseen open models.**

   - **High-quality sample selection (Section 5.3).**  
     We evaluate SpeechJudge-GRM on **Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Talker)**, a separate
     TTS model for several Qwen's proprietary speakers, which is **not used in SpeechJudge-Data**.
     GRM is asked to rank multiple candidates per text. Human evaluation
     (Figure 5) shows that GRM’s selections are consistently preferred, which
     indicates it can identify more natural samples from a new, unseen
     generator.

   - **Post-training generalization (Section 5.4).**  
     We use SpeechJudge-GRM as a reward to post-train **Qwen2.5-0.5B-TTS**, a
     zero-shot TTS model that also **does not participate in data
     construction**. Evaluations on **SeedTTS-Eval** and **Amphion-TTS-Eval**
     (external benchmarks with human reference prompts) show that GRM-based
     post-training improves both text accuracy (T-ACC) and perceived
     naturalness (N-CMOS) over the base model and over a DPO baseline. This
     suggests that GRM’s signal is useful beyond the TTS architectures seen in
     SpeechJudge-Data.

3. **New OOD experiment in the revision: human vs. commercial SeedTTS clones.**

   To further probe generalization to **real speech and stronger, unseen
   generators**, we add a new evaluation in **Appendix G.1 (Table 11)**:

   - We record **500 utterances** from **two native English voice actors**.  
   - Using the **[commercial SeedTTS voice-cloning API](https://www.volcengine.com/product/voicecloning)**, we synthesize clones
     of each recording (SeedTTS is a strong proprietary model not used in
     our training).  
   - Each pair is **(Human recording, SeedTTS clone)**, and we treat the human
     as the more natural reference.

   Neither **SeedTTS** nor these human recordings are present in
   SpeechJudge-Data, making this a **strictly out-of-distribution** test.

   The key results are:

   | Model               | Character 1 | Character 2 | Avg  |
   |---------------------|-----------:|-----------:|-----:|
   | Qwen2.5-Omni-7B     | 48.0       | 44.8       | 46.4 |
   | SpeechJudge-BTRM    | 55.6       | 45.2       | 50.4 |
   | SpeechJudge-GRM     | 57.6       | 67.2       | 62.4 |
   | w/ Voting@10        | 59.8       | 67.5       | 63.7 |

   We observe:

   - The **zero-shot AudioLLM judge** (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) performs around chance
     (46.4%).  
   - The **Bradley–Terry reward model (BTRM)**, which does very well on
     in-distribution SpeechJudge-Eval (72.7%), also collapses toward random
     guessing (50.4%) in this OOD human-vs-clone setting.  
   - In contrast, **SpeechJudge-GRM reaches 62.4% (63.7% with Voting@10)**—
     clearly above chance and substantially better than BTRM—even though it
     has never seen SeedTTS or real human recordings in training.

   This experiment suggests that our two-stage training
   (**SFT + RLVR on human preferences**) allows GRM to capture a **more
   general notion of naturalness** that transfers to **new architectures and
   real speech**, rather than memorizing artifacts of the six training models.

We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed and critical feedback. Many of the
concerns helped us substantially improve the clarity and analysis of the
paper. Below we respond point-by-point and highlight changes in the revised
manuscript (new text is in blue in the PDF).

```
1. On the definition and operationalization of “naturalness” and cases where both audios are unnatural
```

*Comment (summarized):* The concept of “naturalness” is not operationally
defined. It is unclear whether annotators were instructed to consider specific
dimensions (prosody, timing, articulation, spectral quality, etc.). The data
are ordinal preferences rather than metric scores, which can be problematic
when both audios are of low quality (e.g., the “24” example on the website).
There is also no evidence that annotators followed consistent criteria or
MOS/CMOS-like standards. Did the authors analyze cases where both audios were
judged unnatural?

*Response:* We thank the reviewer for carefully raising this fundamental
question. We would first like to clarify that **the operational definition of
naturalness and potential sources of variability are already described in the
paper (Appendix C)**. Here, we would like to clarify why we explicitly position SpeechJudge-Data as an RLHF-style preference dataset rather than as a traditional MOS annotation corpus.

---

### (a) Operational definition of “naturalness” in our annotation protocol

Annotators are **not** asked to make unconstrained, vague choices. The task
introduction and guideline (detailed in
**Appendix C**) explicitly define naturalness along several perceptual
dimensions, including:

- presence of **robotic/electronic tones** and other synthetic artifacts;
- **prosody and intonation** (overly flat vs. exaggerated, unnatural pitch
  movements);
- **speaking rhythm and pauses** (choppy, rushed, or unnaturally long
  silences);
- **word stress and emphasis**;
- and the degree to which the speech “**sounds like a human reading the
  sentence naturally**” in the intended style.

We also distinguish **minor content errors** from truly distracting ones:

> “If there are minor errors in individual words, please do not let them
> affect your overall judgment of naturalness. However, if a large number of
> content errors are found that severely interfere with your listening
> experience, this should affect the audio’s naturalness.”

Conceptually, this is closely aligned with standard **MOS/CMOS protocols** in
TTS, which also ask listeners to rate overall quality/naturalness while
implicitly aggregating over prosody, articulation, and artifacts. In the
revision, we will move a concise summary of these criteria (with examples) from
Appendix C into the main text, to make the operational meaning of
“naturalness” clearer.

---

### (b) Why we use pairwise, ordinal preferences instead of absolute scores

We **intentionally** adopt **pairwise comparisons** (“A vs. B”) rather than
direct 1–5 MOS scores, following standard practice in **RLHF-style human preference
datasets**:

- Each label is an **ordinal preference** (“A more natural” or “B more natural”), which is exactly what **Bradley–Terry reward models, DPO-style
  objectives, and our GRM training** are designed to consume.
- This mirrors how **reward models in text and vision RLHF** are typically
  defined: conditioned on a **given prompt**, ranking **multiple completions
  of the same input**, rather than producing globally calibrated absolute
  scores across prompts.

We do **not** claim to obtain a calibrated, metric MOS value per utterance in
this work. Instead, we focus on learning a **preference-based judge** that can
rank realizations of the **same script** by perceived naturalness, so that it
can be:

- used as a **reward function** for post-training a TTS model (Section 5.4),
- and used for **best-of-N selection** (Figure 5) over multiple generations
  of the same prompt.

---

### (c) Cases where both audios are unnatural and the role of “Tie”

We agree that pairs where **both audios are of low quality** are challenging.
Our interface explicitly allows a **“Tie”** option, including when:

- there is **no perceptible preference**, or  
- both clips are judged **similarly unnatural**.

In early analysis, we observed that such difficult pairs often correspond to:

- **hard prompts for current TTS models**, e.g.  
  – extreme expressive styles (very high or unstable F0),  
  – whisper or heavily stylized voices,  
  – challenging code-switching texts,  
  – or scripts with rich paralinguistic content (laughing, crying, etc.);
- or **utterances with different types of defects**, where one may have
  severe noise but decent prosody, while the other has cleaner acoustics but
  poor articulation or prosody—making “less unnatural” genuinely ambiguous.

```
2. Comparison with stronger / prompt-optimized AudioLLM judges
```

*Comment (summarized):* The evaluation focuses on zero-shot AudioLLMs with
basic prompts. It would be more informative to compare against fine-tuned or
prompt-optimized AudioLLM judges (e.g., AudioJudge). Also, since some
AudioLLMs degrade under CoT prompting, did the authors explore alternative
prompting strategies (e.g., few-shot examples), and what were the results?

*Response:* We appreciate this suggestion. We would like to clarify that our work already includes fine-tuned AudioLLM judges, and in the revision we further report additional prompt-engineering experiments (including few-shot prompting), which we
summarize below.

---

### (a) Fine-tuned AudioLLM judges

We would like to clarify that **both SpeechJudge-BTRM and SpeechJudge-GRM are
fine-tuned AudioLLM judges**:

- They are all based on **Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Thinker)**, a strong open-source
  AudioLLM.
- **SpeechJudge-BTRM** replaces the LM head with a reward prediction head
  and fine-tunes on SpeechJudge-Data.
- **SpeechJudge-GRM** fine-tunes the same backbone in a **generative reward
  modeling** style, first via SFT on CoT+preference data and then via RLVR.

We will make this clearer in Section 5 so that the comparison is not seen as
only against zero-shot AudioLLMs.

---

### (b) Prompt engineering for Qwen2.5-Omni-7B

Before deciding on the “score” prompt used in Table 2, we ran preliminary
experiments with several prompt styles for **Qwen2.5-Omni-7B** on
SpeechJudge-Eval:

Table: **Effect of different prompts for Qwen2.5-Omni-7B.**

| Prompt type          | Regular | Expressive | Total |
|----------------------|:-------:|:---------:|:-----:|
| Rank prompt          |  54.1   |   45.2    | 48.7  |
| Score prompt         |  62.0   |   59.7    | 60.6  |
| Score prompt (CoT)   |  54.4   |   50.6    | 52.9  |

- **Rank prompt:** directly asks “which is more natural, A or B?”.  
- **Score prompt:** asks the model to assign a 1–10 naturalness score to each
  audio and then compares scores. This is exactly the *plain* prompt that is presented in Table 2.  
- **Score prompt (CoT):** same as score prompt but with explicit CoT
  reasoning. This is exactly the *CoT* prompt that is presented in Table 2.  

We find that Qwen2.5-Omni-7B is **highly sensitive to the prompt**: both the
simple rank prompt and the CoT-style score prompt perform close to random
guessing (≈50%), whereas the plain score prompt yields the best (still modest)
accuracy of **60.6%**. Based on the above, we report all of the AudioLLM baselines in the Table 2 using this score prompt.

---

### (c) Few-shot prompting experiments (new in the revision)

Motivated by the reviewer’s suggestion and by work such as AudioJudge, we
further explored **few-shot prompting** for Qwen2.5-Omni-7B. In **Appendix E.2**
we construct \(k\)-shot prompts by prepending \(k\) labeled examples (text +
two audios + naturalness label) to the same score-style instruction. Results
on SpeechJudge-Eval are:

Table: **Performance of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with different \(k\)-shot prompts.**

| Model                         | Regular | Expressive | Total |
|-------------------------------|:-------:|:---------:|:-----:|
| 0-shot      |  62.0   |   59.7    | 60.6  |
| 2-shot                     |  50.9   |   46.6    | 48.2  |
| 4-shot                     |  46.1   |   52.0    | 49.6  |
| 6-shot                     |  50.3   |   53.0    | 51.9  |
| 8-shot                     |  51.0   |   54.8    | 53.3  |
| 16-shot                    |  48.6   |   53.0    | 51.3  |

Contrary to the usual expectation that few-shot prompting should help, **none
of the \(k\)-shot configurations outperforms the 0-shot baseline**. In fact,
accuracy drops from **60.6%** (0-shot) to **48–53%** with few-shot prompts,
with the degradation particularly pronounced on regular speech.

These results are consistent with our observations on CoT prompting:
current open-source AudioLLMs (including Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) still have limited

- instruction-following / format adherence,
- multi-audio comparison ability, and
- long-context handling.

Although few-shot prompts supply more information in principle, the model
struggles to reliably associate multiple text–audio pairs with their labels in
context.

---

### (d) Relation to AudioJudge and scope of this work

AudioJudge is an excellent example showing that **carefully engineered prompts
can significantly improve zero-shot judging**. However, it was released very
close to our submission deadline, and a thorough empirical comparison is
challenging within the current review cycle. Conceptually, our contribution is
orthogonal and complementary:

- **Prompt engineering** aims to push a *frozen* AudioLLM judge to behave
  better.  
- **SpeechJudge-GRM** focuses on **training a reward model from human
  preference data**, using a generative formulation and two-stage SFT+RL
  alignment to better model human naturalness judgments.

```
2. Code-switched speech is harder to generate/evaluate
```

*Comment (summarized):* Code-switched speech is much more difficult for TTS
systems (e.g., CS-FLEURS). This should be addressed directly, and results
could be stratified for ZH/EN/code-switched subsets.

*Response:* We agree that Chinese–English code-switching is a particularly
challenging setting. To keep the quality of the mixed subset reasonably high,
for code-switched data we rely on two advanced, code-switching–enhanced systems, **CosyVoice2-INTP** and **Ints-INTP** [7], which are specifically post-trained for Chinese–English code-switching scenarios. 

Regarding how this difficulty appears in the **annotations** and in
**SpeechJudge-GRM’s performance**, we added detailed language-wise agreement statistics in Appendix C.2 and language-wise evaluation results (including code-switched settings) in Appendix G.1, where code-switched subsets indeed emerge as among the hardest for both annotators and models.

```
3. Choice and representativeness of the six source TTS models
```

*Comment:* What motivated the choice of those six models? Are they representative enough that evaluators trained on this data will have validity across new models?

*Response:* We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Our choice
was driven by both **architectural diversity** and **practical generalization**:

1. **Motivation: diverse, strong generators rather than a single family.**  
   We intentionally selected six advanced open-source TTS systems that cover
   three major generation paradigms:
   - **Auto-regressive (AR):** CosyVoice2, ARS  
   - **Flow-matching (FM):** F5-TTS  
   - **Masked generative models (MGM):** MaskGCT  
   plus two **intelligibility-enhanced** variants, **CosyVoice2-INTP** and
   **Ints-INTP**.  
   This mixture avoids overfitting to artifacts of a single architecture and
   ensures that the reward model must learn higher-level naturalness cues
   (like prosody, rhythm, and expressiveness) beyond trivial pronunciation errors.

2. **Evidence in the original submission: generalization to unseen open models.**  
   We already evaluate SpeechJudge-GRM on models that are **not** used to
   build SpeechJudge-Data:
   - **High-Quality Sample Selection (Section 5.3):** We tested on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Talker), a speech generation model for several Qwen's internal speakers. We find that even though this model and its speakers are completely unseen, SpeechJudge-GRM successfully identified more natural samples (Figure 5).  
   - **Post-training Generalization (Section 5.4):** We used the SpeechJudge-GRM to post-train Qwen2.5-0.5B-TTS, a separate zero-shot TTS model that does not participate in the construction of SpeechJudge-Data. Evaluations on SeedTTS-Eval and Amphion-TTS-Eval show that GRM-based post-training improves both intelligibility
     and perceived naturalness, showing that the reward model transfers to new
     generators and external benchmark.

3. **New experiment in the revision: human vs. commercial SeedTTS clones.**  
   To further test validity across unseen, *stronger* systems, we added a new
   OOD evaluation in **Appendix G.1 (Table 11)**. We record 500 utterances
   from two native English voice actors and synthesize voice clones with **[the
   commercial SeedTTS API](https://www.volcengine.com/product/voicecloning) (a SOTA proprietary model)**. Each test pair is
   (Human recording vs SeedTTS clone); the human recording is treated as the
   more natural reference. Neither SeedTTS nor these human recordings appear
   in SpeechJudge-Data. Results are as follows:

   | Model                 | Character1 | Character2 | Avg  |
   |-----------------------|-----------:|-----------:|-----:|
   | Qwen2.5-Omni-7B       | 48.0       | 44.8       | 46.4 |
   | SpeechJudge-BTRM      | 55.6       | 45.2       | 50.4 |
   | SpeechJudge-GRM       | 57.6       | 67.2       | 62.4 |
   | w/ Voting@10          | 59.8       | 67.5       | 63.7 |

   We can observe that the zero-shot judge (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) is close to chance, and the
   Bradley–Terry reward model (BTRM), despite achieving 72.7% on
   SpeechJudge-Eval (Table 3), also collapses toward random guessing (50.4%) in such OOD evaluation. In
   contrast, **SpeechJudge-GRM reaches 62.4% (63.7% with Voting@10)**, clearly
   above chance and substantially better than BTRM, even though neither
   SeedTTS nor human recordings were used in training.  
   This OOD experiment suggests that our two-stage training (SFT + RLVR)
   enables GRM to capture a *generalizable* notion of naturalness that transfers
   to **new architectures and real speech**, rather than memorizing artifacts
   of the six training models.

We have added these clarifications and the new human-vs-clone results to the
revised paper (Appendix G.1).

We see combining the two directions—e.g., using AudioJudge-style prompts as
inputs to a GRM, or applying our GRM training recipe to other AudioLLM
backbones—as a promising avenue for future work. We will clarify this
distinction and our new few-shot findings in the revised manuscript.

```
3. Annotation bias (linguistic / cultural) and its impact
```

*Comment (summarized):* Although inter-annotator agreement is analyzed, the
paper does not explore potential linguistic or cultural biases in the human
annotations, which could affect the reliability of the dataset and the
alignment of the model with diverse human preferences.

*Response:* We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. In the revised paper
we explicitly analyze and discuss these issues:

---

### (a) Language-wise agreement and potential linguistic bias

We added **Appendix C.2 “Inter-Annotator Agreement”**, where we compute
inter-annotator agreement for **SpeechJudge-Data (pref)** separately for
English, Chinese, and code-switched subsets, and compare them to standard
RLHF datasets in text and vision:

| Subset / Dataset             | Inter-Annotator Agreement |
|------------------------------|---------------------------|
| English (en)                 | 61.4%                     |
| Chinese (zh)                 | 74.1%                     |
| Code-switching (mixed)       | 62.5%                     |
| **Total (SpeechJudge-Data)** | **69.0%**                 |
| InstructGPT [1]              | 72.6%                     |
| ImageReward [2]              | 65.3%                     |

Two observations are relevant to bias:

1. **Overall level.** The overall agreement of **69%** is **comparable to
   widely used RLHF corpora** in other modalities (Text: InstructGPT [1] 72.6%; Vision: ImageReward [2] 65.3%), suggesting that the dataset has a similar reliability
   level to existing RLHF-style human preference datasets.

2. **Language asymmetry.** Despite requiring all annotators who label English
   and Code-switching samples to have **CET-6–level English proficiency or higher**
   (Appendix C.1), agreement is **noticeably higher on English than on Chinese
   and code-switched subsets**. This indicates that certain conditions
   (especially code-switched speech) are more subjective and may be
   perceived differently by our annotator population.

In **Appendix G.1**, we further show that **SpeechJudge-GRM’s accuracy is
also higher on some language conditions than others**, mirroring the agreement
patterns and suggesting that the learned reward model inherits part of this
linguistic bias from the data.

---

### (b) Cultural / population bias and explicit limitation

In the revised **Section 6 “Limitations and Future Work”** and in the
discussion around Appendices C.2 and G.1, we now explicitly state that:

> our annotators are professional raters in China (native Mandarin speakers
> with high but still L2 English proficiency), and inter-annotator agreement
> varies across language subsets. As a result, the current dataset primarily
> reflects the preferences of Chinese and Chinese–English bilingual listeners.

We highlight as an important direction to **extend SpeechJudge-Data to more
languages, cultures, and listener populations**, including **native English
speakers, stronger bilingual annotators, and speakers of additional
languages**, so that future versions of SpeechJudge-GRM can better reflect
diverse cross-cultural notions of “naturalness” and reduce potential
linguistic/cultural bias.

We hope these new analyses and explicit limitations address the reviewer’s
concern about annotation bias and its impact on the dataset and model.

There are two key observations:

1. **Overall level.** The overall agreement of **69%** is **comparable to
   widely used RLHF corpora** in other modalities (InstructGPT 72.6% in text;
   ImageReward 65.3% in vision). This suggests that, as a human preference
   dataset, SpeechJudge-Data has a similar reliability level to existing,
   widely adopted RLHF datasets.

2. **Language asymmetry.**  
   Even though annotators who work on English / mixed data are required to
   have **CET-6–level English proficiency (or higher)**, agreement is
   **noticeably higher on Chinese (74.1%) than on English (61.4%) and
   code-switching (62.5%) subsets**. This confirms that:
   - L2 English and especially **code-switched speech** are more subjective
     and harder to judge consistently for our annotator population, and  
   - the resulting preference data inherently carries **language-specific
     variability**.

In **Appendix G.1**, we further show that **SpeechJudge-GRM’s accuracy on
SpeechJudge-Eval mirrors these trends**: performance is higher on Chinese
pairs than on English and mixed pairs. This indicates that the reward model
naturally inherits part of the **linguistic bias and difficulty structure**
present in the human annotations.

---

### (c) Cultural / population bias and how we position the dataset

In the revised **Section 6 “Limitations and Future Work”** and in the
discussion around Appendices C.2 and G.1, we now state this explicitly:

> our annotators are professional raters in China (native Mandarin speakers
> with high but still L2 English proficiency), and inter-annotator agreement
> is higher on Chinese than on English and mixed subsets. As a result, the
> current dataset primarily reflects the preferences of **Chinese and
> Chinese–English bilingual listeners**, rather than a globally balanced
> listener population.

We highlight as important future work:

- **Extending SpeechJudge-Data to more languages and cultures**, including
  native English speakers, stronger bilingual annotators, and listeners from
  additional language communities; and  
- Designing evaluation subsets and follow-up studies that specifically probe
  **cross-cultural differences in “naturalness”**, rather than treating our
  current annotator pool as universally representative.

In summary, the revised paper now (i) details **per-annotator consistency and
filtering**, (ii) provides **language-wise reliability statistics**, and (iii) explicitly acknowledges and discusses the
**cultural and linguistic bias** inherent in the current annotator population.

```
4. Overreliance on Gemini-2.5-Flash and potential CoT-style bias
```

*Comment (summarized):* The teacher for generating CoT rationales
(Gemini-2.5-Flash) is proprietary, which may undermine reproducibility and the
claim of “openness.” In addition, CoT reasoning might introduce bias by
inheriting the teacher’s explanation style.

*Response:* We appreciate the reviewer’s concerns. Gemini-2.5-Flash is indeed
a closed model; however, in our pipeline its role is **limited, offline, and
replaceable**, and we design both the training procedure and the release so
that its use does **not** prevent reproducibility nor fully determine the
final model’s behavior.

---

### (a) Role of Gemini-2.5-Flash and reproducibility

Gemini-2.5-Flash is used **only once**, as a teacher to generate CoT-style
rationales for the **first SFT stage**:

- Our goal is **not** to distill Gemini itself, but to **bootstrap
  Qwen2.5-Omni-7B’s instruction-following and “analysis + decision” format**,
  so that the subsequent RLVR stage can focus on aligning the reward model
  with **human preferences**.
- Importantly, we **filter teacher outputs with human labels**:
  - For each pair, we **keep** Gemini’s CoT **only if** its final preference
    agrees with the aggregated human label.  
  - Pairs where Gemini disagrees with humans are **excluded from SFT** and are
    used only in the **RLVR stage**, where supervision comes **directly from
    human preferences**, not from the teacher.

Thus, SFT leverages Gemini only on examples where it already behaves
**human-aligned**, and the final SpeechJudge-GRM is trained and evaluated
**without any dependence on Gemini at inference time**.

To address reproducibility, we will release:

- all **CoT supervision actually used for SFT** (prompt, inputs, and
  Gemini-generated rationales that passed the human-agreement filter), and  
- our **training code and GRM checkpoints**.

This allows others to:

1. **Reproduce our SFT+RLVR pipeline without calling Gemini** (simply loading
   the released CoT data), and  
2. **Replace the teacher** with an open-source AudioLLM or human-written
   rationales while reusing the same human preference data.

TTS** (no user-contributed or clinical data), and we did not collect any
personally identifying information beyond the vendor’s internal worker IDs.

The vendor required all annotators to **sign a written informed consent**
agreement before participation, covering the nature of the task, use of the
data for research, compensation scheme, and the fact that only synthetic
speech would be rated. Annotators were adults, could stop at any time, and
were compensated at or above local market rates.

We added a clarifying sentence to the **Ethics Statement** section
of the paper along the lines of:

> “All human annotations were collected from professional annotators recruited
> by a third-party data annotation company under written informed consent, on
> synthetic TTS audio only, with no collection of personally identifying
> information.”

We hope this directly addresses the reviewer’s concern about human-subjects
oversight and consent.

### References

> [1] Ouyang, Long, et al. "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback." NeurIPS 2022.
> 
> [2] Xu, Jiazheng, et al. "Imagereward: Learning and evaluating human preferences for text-to-image generation." NeurIPS 2023.
> 
> [3] Krippendorff, Klaus. Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology. Sage publications, 2018.
> 
> [4] Ohmura, Junki, et al. "LibriTTS-VI: A Public Corpus and Novel Methods for Efficient Voice Impression Control." arXiv:2509.15626.
> 
> [5] Perepelkina Olga, et al. "RAMAS: Russian multimodal corpus of dyadic interaction for affective computing." International Conference on Speech and Computer. Cham: Springer International Publishing, 2018.
> 
> [6] Bruder Camila, et al. "Perceptual (but not acoustic) features predict singing voice preferences." Scientific reports 14.1 (2024).
> 
> [7] Zhang, Xueyao, et al. "Advancing zero-shot text-to-speech intelligibility across diverse domains via preference alignment." ACL 2025.

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and suggestions. Below we address each major point and summarize the changes made in the revised paper (highlighted in blue in the PDF).

```
1. Cross-lingual and expressive performance of SpeechJudge-GRM
```

*Comment (summarized):* The dataset includes cross-lingual and expressive samples, but the paper lacks in-depth analysis of how SpeechJudge-GRM performs on these specific subsets (e.g., zh2en vs en2zh, emotional vs accented), which
makes its generalizability to diverse linguistic and stylistic scenarios unclear.

*Response:* We appreciate this suggestion and have added a new subsection **Appendix G.1 “Performance under Different Data Distributions”** in the revision. There we report detailed breakdowns of SpeechJudge-GRM (and all
baselines) across **language configurations** and **prompt styles**. Below we highlight two key tables.

---

### (a) Expressive subset: cross-lingual settings

Table 9 (Appendix G.1): **Accuracy on SpeechJudge-Eval (expressive) across language settings.**

| Model                    | en2en | zh2en | zh2zh | en2zh | en2mixed | zh2mixed | Avg  |
|--------------------------|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:-------:|:--------:|:----:|
| Qwen2.5-Omni-7B          | 43.6 | 51.7 | 61.1 | 70.9 |  64.5   |  69.6    | 59.7 |
| Gemini-2.5-Flash         | 53.6 | 68.3 | 73.3 | 76.4 |  64.5   |  67.1    | 66.2 |
| SpeechJudge-BTRM         | 62.9 | 56.7 | 72.2 | 85.5 |  68.6   |  67.1    | 69.5 |
| SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT)    | 61.4 | 66.7 | 89.1 | 77.8 |  74.4   |  73.4    | 73.7 |

**Observations:**

- In the expressive subset: Chinese-involving settings (zh2zh, zh2mixed) tend to be easier than en2en. For example,
  SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL) with Voting@10 attains **82.2% on zh2zh** and
  **84.8% on zh2mixed**, compared to **75.0% on en2en**. This aligns with the **inter-annotator agreement analysis in Appendix C.2**, where
  expressive and code-switched English subsets show lower human agreement, and
  also reflects the increased linguistic/prosodic complexity of expressive and
  mixed speech.
- Importantly, **GRM maintains a clear advantage** over BTRM and AudioLLMs
  across *all* language settings, indicating that its relative strength is
  robust to cross-lingual variation.

---

### (b) Prompt styles: regular vs emotional / accented / whisper / game

Table 10 (Appendix G.1): **Accuracy on SpeechJudge-Eval across prompt styles.**

| Model                    | Regular | Emotional | Accented | Whisper | Game |
|--------------------------|:-------:|:---------:|:--------:|:-------:|:----:|
| Qwen2.5-Omni-7B          |  61.0   |   56.7    |   64.4   |  57.1   | 61.3 |
| Gemini-2.5-Flash         |  72.8   |   63.7    |   66.7   |  74.6   | 66.0 |
| SpeechJudge-BTRM         |  77.5   |   69.8    |   71.3   |  76.2   | 66.8 |
| SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT)    |  77.8   |   75.3    |   80.5   |  71.4   | 70.2 |
|    w/ Voting@10            |  77.3   |   76.7    |   80.5   |  74.6   | 78.7 |
| SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL) |  79.0   |   74.4    |   81.6   |  79.4   | 74.5 |
|    w/ Voting@10            |  80.5   |   78.1    |   85.1   |  82.5   | 75.7 |

**Observations:**

- For **SpeechJudge-BTRM**, regular prompts are the easiest (77.5%), while
  emotional and game-character styles are notably harder (69.8% and 66.8%).
- In contrast, **SpeechJudge-GRM benefits more from expressive conditions**:
  with SFT+RL and Voting@10, GRM achieves **80.5% on regular**, but rises to
  **85.1% on accented** and **82.5% on whisper** prompts, and also narrows the
  gap on emotional and game prompts (from ~10 points for BTRM to only a few
  points).
- We believe this reflects the advantage of the **generative reward model**
  and its **CoT-based training**: by explicitly reasoning about artifacts,
  prosody, and style, GRM is better able to handle challenging conditions such
  as accented speech and whisper, rather than overfitting to the most frequent
  regular style.

---

### (c) Additional OOD evidence

Beyond these in-distribution analyses, **Appendix G.1** also introduces a new
OOD benchmark on **human recordings vs commercial SeedTTS voice clones**. On
this highly challenging setting (real speakers and a strong proprietary TTS
never seen during training), SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL) still clearly
outperforms BTRM and generic AudioLLMs, suggesting that the learned notion of
naturalness generalizes not only across **languages and styles** within
SpeechJudge-Eval but also across **unseen architectures and real speech**.

We hope these new results address the reviewer’s request for a more systematic
analysis of cross-lingual, expressive, and more different scenarios.

We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments and for engaging deeply with
both the dataset and model aspects of our work. We summarize below how we
address each point; all new or modified text is highlighted in blue in the
revised PDF.

```
1. Using “expressiveness” as an additional evaluation dimension
```

*Comment (summarized):* The corpus contains both regular and expressive
samples, but the evaluation focuses only on naturalness. Could expressiveness
itself be an evaluation dimension?

*Response:* We appreciate this suggestion. We agree that **expressiveness is a
crucial aspect of speech quality**, and this is precisely why we designed
SpeechJudge-Data/SpeechJudge-Eval to include expressive categories (emotional,
accented, whisper, game) in addition to regular speech.

In the current work, however, we **deliberately restrict the target signal to
“overall naturalness”** and use expressive prompts primarily to **stress-test
naturalness judgment** rather than to define a second target dimension:

- Annotators are instructed (Appendix C) to judge **“which audio sounds more
  natural overall”**, considering prosody, rhythm, articulation, etc. They are
  *not* asked “which audio is more expressive”.  
- Expressive styles enter our study as **challenging conditions**: in the
  revision, **Appendix G.1 (Tables 9–10)** analyzes performance separately on
  regular vs. expressive subsets and across expressive styles. We observe that
  expressive speech is generally harder for all models, but SpeechJudge-GRM
  maintains a clear advantage over baselines in these subsets as well.

We fully agree that **treating expressiveness as a separate evaluation
dimension** would be very valuable and is naturally supported by the data, but
we believe this requires **additional, dedicated annotation**:

- A clear protocol distinguishing *appropriate expressiveness* from
  *over-acting* or *stylistic preference* (which may decrease perceived
  naturalness for some listeners).
- Calibration examples and reliability analysis specifically for
  “expressiveness” labels, so that we do not conflate genuine expressive
  quality with annotators’ cultural or personal style preferences.
- Potentially a **multi-dimensional reward model** that predicts both
  naturalness and expressiveness (or a separate “expressiveness judge”).

We now explicitly mention this in **Section 6 (Limitations and Future Work)**:
the current work focuses on a **single naturalness dimension**, and extending
SpeechJudge-Data with **explicit expressiveness annotations and a
multi-dimensional reward model** is an important direction that we plan to
pursue in follow-up work.

```
2. Treatment of “tie” labels and release of individual annotations
```

*Comment (summarized):* The paper excludes “tie” labels from both the training
data and the evaluation benchmark. It might be valuable for the model to
recognize when two samples are of similar naturalness. Given the observed
annotator disagreement, releasing individual ratings (not just majority votes)
would also enable studying variability and perceptual uncertainty.

*Response:* We fully agree that ties and annotator variability are important
for understanding perceptual uncertainty. Our current design choices follow
standard RLHF practice, but we see tie-aware modeling as a natural extension
of SpeechJudge and will open all the individual ratings during our data release.

---

### (a) Why we exclude “tie” pairs in this work

We made this design choice **primarily to stay aligned with standard RLHF
objectives**. Most existing reward-model / preference-alignment methods (e.g.,
Bradley-Terry reward models, DPO-style alignment) are formulated on **binary
winner–loser pairs**. To keep the comparison clean and to clearly highlight
our modeling contribution (GRM vs. BTRM, and SFT+RL vs. classic BT training),
we adopt this widely used binary setting in the main experiments, rather than
introducing a custom tie-aware objective in this first work.

---

### (b) Why ties are interesting and how we plan to use them

We agree with the reviewer that **explicitly modeling ties is valuable**:
recognizing “no perceptible difference” would give a more nuanced view of
perceptual similarity and uncertainty.

Importantly, our annotation pipeline already collects **extra information for
tie cases**: **when raters choose “Tie”, they further select *why*, with options
such as “both very good” or “both not good”**. These metadata could
support future work on separating “equally high-quality” vs “equally poor”
ties, or on reducing reliance on pairwise comparisons and moving toward
quality-aware scoring (such as KTO-style approaches [3]). 

Properly exploiting ties typically requires going beyond standard binary
BTRM/DPO objectives to ternary or tie-aware preference models [4,5]. We see this as a promising direction and will explicitly highlight **tie-aware
preference modeling** as an important avenue for future work.

We thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback. In the revised
manuscript we have incorporated additional analyses and clarifications; **all
new or modified text is highlighted in blue in the PDF** for easy inspection.

### Main changes

1. **Section 6 - Limitations and Future Work.**  
   We added an explicit limitations section discussing  
   - the scope of our data and annotator population (language coverage and L2/L1 effects),  
   - typical failure modes of SpeechJudge-GRM,  
   - potential bias and incompleteness of the CoT supervision from Gemini-2.5-Flash, and  
   - the current utterance-level (coarse-grained) formulation versus future fine-grained, segment-level naturalness modeling.

2. **Appendix C.2 – Inter-Annotator Agreement.**  
   We added a new subsection with dataset-level inter-annotator agreement analysis, including:  
   - ternary vs. binary preference labels on SpeechJudge-Data (raw vs. pref),  
   - breakdown by language and prompt style, and  
   - comparison with standard RLHF datasets in text and vision (e.g., InstructGPT, ImageReward).  
   This directly addresses questions about annotation reliability, L2/L1 differences, and potential cultural bias.

3. **Appendix E.2 – Few-Shot Prompting for AudioLLM Judges.**  
   Beyond the CoT prompting study in Appendix E.1, we now evaluate *k*-shot in-context prompting for Qwen2.5-Omni-7B on SpeechJudge-Eval.  
   The results show that few-shot prompting does **not** improve over the zero-shot baseline and often degrades accuracy, reinforcing our motivation for training dedicated reward models rather than relying solely on prompt engineering.

4. **Appendix G – More Evaluation Results for SpeechJudge-GRM.**  
   We introduced a new appendix with three subsections:
   - **G.1 Performance under Different Data Distributions.**  
     Detailed breakdowns of SpeechJudge-Eval by language pair and prompt style, plus a new ***out-of-distribution*** benchmark on human recordings vs. commercial SeedTTS voice clones.  
     These experiments show that SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL) generalizes better than BTRM and generic AudioLLMs on this challenging setting.
   - **G.2 Quality Analysis of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning.**  
     (i) An automatic consistency check of CoT reasoning vs. final decisions using DeepSeek-V3, and  
     (ii) a human study of CoT faithfulness across Gemini-2.5-Flash, SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT), and SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL), as well as qualitative comparisons of reasoning style using strong text LLMs.
   - **G.3 Error Analysis of SpeechJudge-GRM.**  
     Qualitative inspection of remaining failure cases on SpeechJudge-Eval, highlighting common patterns (clean vs. lively speech, prosody vs. articulation trade-offs, extreme expressive styles, and very small preference gaps).

These revisions are intended to address concerns raised in the reviews about
annotation reliability and bias, AudioLLM baselines and prompting strategies,
CoT quality, and generalization—especially to real speech and strong
commercial TTS systems. The core methodology and the main conclusions of the
paper remain unchanged.

In the current study:

- These **Tie** cases receive explicit labels and a follow-up “why tie?” questionnaire from human annotators in our **SpeechJudge-Data (raw)**.  
- For **SpeechJudge-Data (pref)** and **SpeechJudge-Eval**, we *exclude* tie
  pairs and focus on clear winner–loser labels to match standard RLHF
  objectives and obtain a cleaner benchmark and preference training data.

We did not perform a separate, large-scale quantitative breakdown of “both
unnatural” vs. “both good” ties in this current version, but we **preserve and
plan to release all raw labels and tie reasons** with the dataset. This will
enable future work on tie-aware and uncertainty-aware preference modeling,
which we now highlight as a direction in **Section 6 (Limitations and Future
Work)**.

---

### (d) Evidence of annotator consistency and calibration

Although we do not calibrate raters to an external MOS corpus, we do check and
enforce consistency:

- **Appendix C.1** describes per-annotator reliability filtering: we compute
  each annotator’s agreement with peers and exclude low-consistency raters
  (<30% agreement) from the final dataset.
- **Appendix C.2** reports **inter-annotator agreement** at the dataset level:
  SpeechJudge-Data (pref) reaches **69%** agreement, comparable to  
  **InstructGPT** (72.6%) in text and **ImageReward** (65.3%) in vision. This situates our variability at a similar level to other widely used RLHF
  datasets.

We will emphasize the following points in the limitation section that:

- SpeechJudge-Data is a **preference dataset**, not a MOS corpus;  
- its labels are **ordinal and prompt-conditioned** by design; and  
- extending it with native raters for more languages and tie-aware modeling
  is an important direction.

We hope this clarification addresses the reviewer’s concerns about the
definition, operationalization, and variability of “naturalness” in our
dataset.

```
2. Synthetic-only training data, bias/circularity, and generalization
```

*Comments (summarized):* The dataset is built entirely from synthetic TTS
outputs with no human ground-truth references, so the reward model might
inherit model-specific artifacts rather than perceptual naturalness. In
addition, the benchmark and the reward model share the same construction
pipeline, raising concerns about circular evaluation and poor generalization.
How do you ensure the model is not overfitting to specific TTS artifacts, and
how generalizable is SpeechJudge-GRM to unseen voices (real human speech) or
out-of-distribution languages?

*Response:* We appreciate the reviewer’s thorough critique. Below we clarify
the design choices behind the synthetic dataset, and present several pieces of
evidence—both from the original submission and from new experiments in the
revised version—that SpeechJudge-GRM does **not** simply memorize artifacts of
the training generators, but learns a transferable notion of naturalness
within its intended language scope.

---

### (a) Why synthetic, same-text pairs (and not human recordings)

SpeechJudge-Data is indeed **fully synthetic**: all ~99K samples are generated
by TTS models (CosyVoice2, F5-TTS, MaskGCT, etc.). This is a **deliberate design choice**, driven by:

1. **Same-transcript pairing.**  
   Our labels are defined on **pairs of utterances with identical transcripts**:
   annotators answer *“for this sentence, which realization sounds more
   natural?”*. This design isolates naturalness from confounds such as text
   content, lexical difficulty, or phonetic coverage.

   Constructing such **same-text, multi-take pairs at scale** from real human
   recordings is extremely difficult and costly: existing speech corpora
   rarely contain multiple high-quality, comparable human recordings of the
   exact same sentence. TTS models, in contrast, make it straightforward to
   sample multiple realizations per text across architectures, sampling
   strategies, and styles.

2. **Intended use as a reward model for TTS post-training.**  
   Our primary goal is a **reward model for TTS post-training**, where the
   policy’s rollouts are themselves synthetic utterances for a given prompt.
   In that setting, the reward model only ever sees *synthetic* candidates and
   must decide which synthetic sample is more natural. Training the judge on
   **synthetic-vs-synthetic** comparisons matches this deployment regime.

---

### (b) Multilingual and code-switched scripts

For the **target texts** paired with these expressive references, we use
**DeepSeek-V3** with a structured prompt (Appendix B.1) that explicitly
controls:

- the **language** (keep zh vs. en, or generate a zh–en mixed version),
- the **writing style** (formal, informal, literary, advertising, etc.), and
- the **length** (roughly 10–20 s of read speech).

We ask DeepSeek-V3 to output (for each reference) a **continuation**, a
**translation**, and a **code-switching** variant where only part of the
content is switched between Chinese and English.

During construction we perform both automatic and manual checks:

- **Language and format checks:** we verify that “zh”, “en”, and “mixed”
  scripts match their intended category using character-set and simple
  language-ID heuristics (e.g., mixed scripts must contain both Han characters
  and Latin words in non-trivial proportion), and drop outputs that violate
  length or format constraints or contain obvious degeneration.
- **Spot-checks for fluency and style:** we manually inspect samples from each
  style / language bucket to confirm that the sentences are fluent, semantically
  coherent, and match the requested style.

Empirically, DeepSeek-V3 produces high-quality texts under these constraints,
and the remaining scripts are linguistically natural and well aligned with
their expressive references.

---

In summary, expressive prompts are based on **curated, style-labeled human
corpora** with additional filtering, while multilingual / code-switched scripts
are **LLM-generated under tight prompt constraints**, automatically screened,
and manually spot-checked. We will clarify these quality-control procedures
explicitly in the revised manuscript.

```
7. Analysis of cases where GRM disagrees with humans
```

*Comment:* Did the authors analyze cases where the GRM and humans disagree—what aspects of speech cause errors?

*Response:* We agree that understanding *why* SpeechJudge-GRM fails is
important. In the revision we added **Appendix G.3 “Error Analysis of
SpeechJudge-GRM”**, where we qualitatively inspect **SpeechJudge-Eval pairs
with high human agreement (FA-level) but incorrect GRM predictions**. The main
patterns are:

- **Over-weighting cleanness vs. liveliness.**  
  In many errors, the human-preferred sample contains mild background noise
  but clearly more human-like prosody and articulation, whereas the other
  clip is cleaner yet more robotic / over-smoothed.  
  GRM sometimes chooses the cleaner audio, suggesting that it can
  over-emphasize acoustic cleanness when humans prioritize liveliness and
  natural prosodic variation.

- **Prosody–articulation trade-offs.**  
  Another frequent pattern is a trade-off between expressive prosody and
  technical correctness. Humans often prefer speech with natural rhythm and
  intonation despite small pronunciation issues, while GRM occasionally
  favors the perfectly articulated but noticeably flatter reading.  
  This indicates that the relative weighting between prosody and articulation
  is not yet fully captured.

- **Extreme expressive styles.**  
  Errors also concentrate in highly expressive conditions.  
  For emotional speech with very high F0 or strong emphasis, annotators view
  the exaggerated prosody as appropriate for the style, but GRM sometimes
  penalizes it as “unnatural” and prefers a neutral rendition.  
  For whisper prompts, the lack of F0 makes prosody assessment difficult; GRM
  occasionally fails to pick the more fluent whisper when both samples sound
  somewhat degraded.

- **Very small preference gaps.**  
  A small subset of mistakes occurs when both clips are high quality and
  differ only in subtle cues (micro-pauses, breathing, slight emphasis
  shifts). In these cases GRM’s choices are effectively close to random,
  which is unsurprising given the weak supervision signal.

Overall, these analyses show that SpeechJudge-GRM’s errors are concentrated on
**nuanced trade-offs** (cleanness vs. liveliness, prosody vs. articulation)
and on **challenging expressive styles**. In the paper we highlight these
observations as guidance for future work, e.g., incorporating explicit
modeling of recording conditions, style-aware priors, and additional targeted
training examples for expressive and borderline cases.

### References

> [1] Ouyang, Long, et al. "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback." NeurIPS 2022.
> 
> [2] Xu, Jiazheng, et al. "Imagereward: Learning and evaluating human preferences for text-to-image generation." NeurIPS 2023.

strengths.value:
Targeted an important open problem: aligning speech generation with perceptual human judgment.
Provides a relatively large corpus (99K pairs) of human preference labels, which could be a useful resource for benchmarking.
Integrates SFT and RLHF (GRPO) techniques for audio reward modeling, which conceptually connects textual RLHF paradigms with audio generation.
Offers comparisons across a broad set of AudioLLMs (Gemini, Qwen, Kimi, GPT-4o), giving some insight into current model limitations.

weaknesses.value:
1. Ill-defined concept of “naturalness”
The central concept of speech naturalness is not operationally defined or quantitatively measured in an absolute or reproducible way. Annotators are instructed to make pairwise comparisons (“which one sounds more natural”), but the paper does not clarify whether they were asked to assess naturalness along specific perceptual dimensions such as prosody, timing, articulation, or spectral quality. As a result, the collected data are ordinal rather than metric, encoding only relative preference (i.e., which sample is less unnatural). This design becomes problematic in cases where both audios are of low quality—for instance, in the example on their project website (“case 1”), both clips mispronounce the word 24, leaving no meaningful basis for determining which is superior. Furthermore, the paper provides no evidence that annotators followed consistent perceptual criteria or were calibrated to established standards such as MOS or CMOS protocols.

2. Dataset built entirely from synthetic TTS outputs. The authors explicitly state that all 99K samples come from synthetic TTS models (CosyVoice2, F5-TTS, MaskGCT, etc.) using synthetic prompts. This raises several issues: No human speech ground truth. The corpus lacks human-recorded references, so the model never learns what “human-like” actually sounds like. Model bias inheritance. Because all training data originate from a small set of TTS architectures, the reward model is likely to internalize architectural artifacts (e.g., vocoder noise, prosody style) rather than perceptual naturalness. Circular evaluation. The benchmark and reward model are both trained and tested on samples generated by the same model family, leading to evaluation leakage and poor generalization

3. Limited analysis of annotation reliability and bias.
While the paper discusses agreement levels (FA/WA/WD/FD), more detail is needed on labeler consistency, potential cultural bias in “naturalness,” and language-specific reliability. For a human-feedback dataset, these issues are central.

4. Overreliance on closed models (Gemini-2.5-Flash).
The teacher model for generating CoT rationales is proprietary. The dependence on a non-reproducible component undermines the claim of full openness and may limit reproducibility of the SFT stage.

5. Statistical analysis of results is thin.
Accuracy gains (e.g., +4.5%) are reported without confidence intervals or significance tests. Given the subjective nature of the task, statistical reliability is important.

The results (Table 13 of Appendix G.2) are:

| Model                    | Prosody & Intonation | Pacing & Rhythm | Articulation & Clarity | Avg       |
|--------------------------|:--------------------:|:---------------:|:----------------------:|:---------:|
| Gemini-2.5-Flash         | 1.90 ± 0.38          | 2.00 ± 0.44     | 2.10 ± 0.43            | 2.00 ± 0.34 |
| SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT)    | 2.00 ± 0.39          | 2.15 ± 0.29     | 1.95 ± 0.42            | 2.03 ± 0.33 |
| SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL) | 2.10 ± 0.20          | 2.00 ± 0.21     | 2.40 ± 0.32            | 2.17 ± 0.12 |

All three models obtain averages around **2.0**, meaning their CoT rationales
are generally meaningful rather than dominated by hallucination. Importantly,
GRM **does not lose CoT quality after distillation**; instead, after RL:

- SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT) slightly improves the average score over the Gemini
  teacher, and  
- SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL) further improves to **2.17 ± 0.12**, with the
  largest gain on **Articulation & Clarity** (2.40 vs. 2.10 for Gemini),
  suggesting that RLVR encourages the model to focus more accurately on
  pronunciation and intelligibility-related artifacts when explaining its
  decisions.

Thus, although RL constrains only the final naturalness reward, it also
**mildly enhances the faithfulness** of the reasoning.

---

### (d) Differences in reasoning style

We also examine *how* the reasoning changes across models. We sample 20
SpeechJudge-Eval cases where all three models predict the correct preference
and feed their CoTs in triplets to **GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3**,
asking them to summarize similarities and systematic differences.

The analyzers broadly agree on the following qualitative picture (**see Appendix G.2 for more details**):

- **Gemini-2.5-Flash:** strongest at linking prosody and rhythm to **semantic
  meaning and discourse structure**, often explaining *why* an intonation
  pattern distorts the intended message.
- **SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT):** emphasizes **human-likeness and expressiveness**
  with stable formatting and a slightly more generous tone, but pays somewhat
  less attention to low-level signal artifacts.
- **SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL):** more **critical and technically oriented**,
  focusing on mispronunciations, noise, and clarity; sometimes blunter in
  wording and slightly less uniform in format, but more explicit about error
  severity.

These observations support our claim that during RL, the model is allowed to
“autonomously optimize its rationale generation”: while the reward uses only
the preference label, the model **adjusts which aspects it emphasizes** to
better match human preferences.

---

### (e) Scope and limitations

We also acknowledge in **Section 6 (Limitations and Future Work)** that:

- Our CoT training inevitably **inherits stylistic bias** from the
  Gemini-generated rationales, since we filter only on the final preference,
  not on every sentence of the explanation.
- We do not yet provide human feedback on CoT *style* itself (only on final
  judgments).

*Response:* We fully agree, and we would like to clarify that a

In **Section 5.4 (Figure 6a)**, we evaluate four post-training methods for

We fully agree with the reviewer that individual ratings are valuable for

- and majority-vote labels used in this paper.

- analyze annotator-specific biases and agreement patterns,  
- experiment with **tie-aware reward models** or mixture-of-raters models, and  
- develop uncertainty-aware metrics on top of SpeechJudge-Data.

```
3. Quality of Gemini-2.5-Flash CoT and reasoning ability of SpeechJudge-GRM
```

*Comment (summarized):* Gemini-2.5-Flash is used as the teacher to generate
CoT data for SFT, but its own accuracy is still suboptimal. Can the authors
say more about the quality of its CoT rationales and any verification they
performed? In addition, during RL only the final naturalness judgment is
constrained—how good is the model’s reasoning ability, and is there any
quantitative / qualitative analysis of its CoT outputs?

*Response:* We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful question. In the revised
version we added **Appendix G.2 “Quality Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
Reasoning”**, which directly addresses these concerns. We summarize the key
points below and reproduce the main tables here for convenience.

---

### (a) Why use Gemini-2.5-Flash as a teacher and how we filter its errors

Although Gemini-2.5-Flash is not perfect on SpeechJudge-Eval
(69.1% accuracy in Table 2), it is **the strongest AudioLLM judge we found
under a unified evaluation protocol**. We use it only in the *first* SFT
stage to cold-start the Qwen2.5-Omni-7B–based GRM.

Crucially, we **filter the teacher data with human labels**:

- We query Gemini with our CoT prompt and **keep a pair only if the final
  preference agrees with the aggregated human label**.
- Pairs where Gemini disagrees with humans are **excluded from SFT** and are
  used only later in the RLVR stage, where training is driven **purely by
  human preferences**, not by the teacher.
- Thus, SFT distills Gemini’s CoT **only on examples where it already behaves
  human-aligned**, and the subsequent RLVR stage allows SpeechJudge-GRM to
  further surpass the teacher.

---

### (b) Logical consistency between reasoning and conclusion

We first ask whether a model’s CoT reasoning is logically compatible with its
final decision. Using **DeepSeek-V3** as a meta-judge, we prompt it to inspect
the CoT analysis of A/B (prosody, rhythm, articulation, overall naturalness)
and the final 1–10 scores, and to decide whether the *preference implied in
the reasoning* matches the model’s final choice.

A prediction is counted as *consistent* if DeepSeek judges the reasoning and
the decision to agree. The results (Table 12 in the paper) are:

| Model                    | Consistency |
|--------------------------|:-----------:|
| Gemini-2.5-Flash         |   97.9%     |
| SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT)    |   97.6%     |
| SpeechJudge-GRM (SFT+RL) |   98.2%     |

All three models show **very high internal consistency**, indicating that
their CoT explanations are not arbitrary stories but align well with their
final naturalness decisions.

---

### (c) Human-rated faithfulness and hallucination

To directly assess faithfulness, we run a **human evaluation** with
experienced speech researchers (details in Appendix G.2). For each sampled
SpeechJudge-Eval pair and each model, experts inspect the CoT and assign a
score from 1–3 on three dimensions (1. Prosody & Intonation; 2. Pacing & Rhythm; 3. Articulation & Clarity. These match the dimensions in our CoT prompt of Table 1):

- **3** = highly sensible (references concrete audio details; analysis correct)  
- **2** = partially sensible (overall good/bad tendency right, some coarse or
  imperfect details)  
- **1** = not sensible / mostly hallucinated.

```
4. Prompt engineering for CoT and the SFT stage
```

*Comment (summarized):* Since some open-source AudioLLMs degrade with CoT
prompts, did the authors explore alternative prompt engineering strategies
(e.g., few-shot prompts) **for the SFT stage**, and what were the results?

*Response:* We agree that CoT prompting does not universally help AudioLLMs.
Indeed, in **Appendix E.1** we show that CoT prompting **improves** the
closed-source Gemini-2.5-Flash on SpeechJudge-Eval, but **hurts** some
open-source AudioLLMs such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and Kimi-Audio-7B-Instruct.

For the **SFT stage of SpeechJudge-GRM**, our setup is slightly different from
inference-time prompting:

- We use **Gemini-2.5-Flash**—one of the strongest AudioLLM judges in our
  evaluation—as a **teacher** to generate CoT-style rationales with a *single,
  carefully designed CoT prompt* (Table 1), decomposing naturalness into
  prosody, rhythm, articulation, and an overall 1–10 score plus final
  preference.
- For this teacher model, CoT prompting **consistently improves naturalness
  judgment accuracy** on SpeechJudge-Eval (Appendix E.1), so the rationales we
  distill into GRM come from a configuration where CoT is beneficial rather
  than harmful.

Our goal in SFT is to **cold-start Qwen2.5-Omni-7B’s instruction-following and
reasoning format**, not to exhaustively tune prompts for the student itself.
Therefore, we deliberately **keep the SFT template fixed and simple**:
the student is trained to imitate Gemini’s CoT outputs under that one prompt.
Once SFT is finished, subsequent **RLVR training uses only human preferences
and no longer depends on the teacher prompt**, which helps GRM move beyond any
residual teacher bias.

In summary, for SFT we intentionally use a single CoT template with a teacher
for which CoT is empirically helpful, and we rely on the subsequent RLVR
stage (trained directly on human preferences) to further refine and
de-bias the reward model. Systematically exploring alternative SFT templates
or few-shot-style SFT supervision is an interesting direction that we leave to
future work.

### References

> [1] Ouyang, Long, et al. "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback." NeurIPS 2022.
> 
> [2] Xu, Jiazheng, et al. "Imagereward: Learning and evaluating human preferences for text-to-image generation." NeurIPS 2023.

4. Details on evaluator recruitment and qualifications
```

*Comment (summarized):* More information about how evaluators were recruited
and screened should appear in the main text, since annotation reliability is
crucial—especially if the dataset is to be used beyond Mandarin.

*Response:* We completely agree that the reliability of the annotation process
is central, not an afterthought. In the revision we both clarified the
procedure and surfaced key details into the main paper.

1. **Annotator recruitment and screening.**

5. “Most-likely-label” predictor
```

*Comment:* What is the score of a most-likely-label predictor? I am assuming that the distribution of labels, particularly after subselecting for only FA data, would not be uniform.

6. Human evaluation vs. proxy metrics in Section 5.4
```

*Comment (summarized):* A true test of the effectiveness of the evaluator for
training would be human evaluation. The current proxies are fine, but showing
improvements in MOS would more directly demonstrate effectiveness.

*Response:* We thank the reviewer for this important point. We fully agree
that the ultimate goal of using SpeechJudge-GRM as a reward is to improve
**human-perceived** speech quality, and that a large-scale MOS-style listening
test would be the most direct evidence.

In Section 5.4 we already include **human evaluation** for the post-trained
TTS systems:

- Figure 6(a) reports a **naturalness CMOS (N-CMOS)** study conducted with
  expert listeners on SeedTTS-Eval and Amphion-TTS-Eval. All post-training
  methods improve perceived naturalness over the base Qwen2.5-0.5B-TTS model,
  and the **SpeechJudge-GRM–based variants achieve the largest gains**.
- Figure 6(b) reports **win/lose/tie ratios for speaker similarity**, showing
  that GRM-based post-training largely preserves speaker identity.

These subjective results already indicate that SpeechJudge-GRM is an
effective training signal in terms of human perception.

That said, we agree that our current human study is **limited in scale and
scope**: it covers only two evaluation sets, about 70 utterances per system,
and expert listeners only, and we do not provide a full absolute MOS test
with a larger and more diverse listener pool. In the revised manuscript we
now explicitly acknowledge this as a limitation in **Section 6
(“Limitations and Future Work”)**, and we highlight conducting a more
comprehensive MOS study as an important direction for future work to further
validate SpeechJudge-GRM as a general-purpose training signal.

These results suggest that:

1. **DPO-style alignment on SpeechJudge-Data is already an effective way to
   model human preferences**, and  
2. **Using SpeechJudge-GRM as a reward model provides additional benefits over
   the DPO baseline**, especially in terms of perceived naturalness, which is
   the main focus of our work.

We will make the DPO nature of the “w/ SpeechJudge-Data” baseline clearer in
the revision to avoid confusion.

```
5. Can SpeechJudge-GRM be used as an absolute MOS predictor?
```

*Comment:* It might be informative to evaluate whether a model trained with SpeechJudge-GRM as the reward model can also predict absolute MOS scores. Since absolute MOS scores are generally more practical and efficient for automatic assessment and benchmarking of TTS quality than pairwise comparisons, such an analysis could further demonstrate the utility of the proposed data and model.

*Response:* We appreciate this suggestion and agree that **absolute MOS scores
are very practical** for many TTS evaluation pipelines. At the same time,
SpeechJudge-Data and SpeechJudge-GRM are **deliberately designed from a
pairwise, text-conditioned perspective**, which makes them fundamentally
different from standard point-wise MOS predictors (e.g., UTMOS-style models).

---

### (a) Why GRM is not directly a global MOS regressor

In **SpeechJudge-Data**, each preference pair \((a_1, a_2)\) is constructed so
that **both audios share the *same transcript***. Annotators are always asked:
*“For this script, which version sounds more natural?”*

This design intentionally isolates naturalness from confounds such as text
content, linguistic difficulty, or phonetic coverage. As a consequence:

- SpeechJudge-GRM is trained only on **within-text comparisons**, learning a
  function that, *for a fixed text*, orders multiple realizations by
  naturalness.
- We **never collect preferences across different transcripts** (e.g., “is
  this sentence with text A more natural than that sentence with text B?”).

This is also consistent with the **standard RLHF setting for reward models**:
in text and vision RLHF, rewards are almost always defined *conditioned on a
given prompt*, comparing multiple completions for the same input rather than
comparing completions across different prompts.

Therefore, the latent “quality scale” learned by GRM is **only defined up to
an arbitrary shift/scale *within each text***. There is no supervision tying
together the scale of sentence \(t_1\) and sentence \(t_2\), so we cannot
calibrate a single, transcript-agnostic 1–5 MOS value in a principled way.

This setup is ideal for our primary use cases:

- **Rewarding TTS post-training** (Section 5.4), where the model generates
  multiple candidates for the *same* text and GRM provides a preference signal
  over those candidates; and  
- **Best-of-N selection** (Figure 5), where GRM ranks several outputs of the
  same prompt and chooses the most natural one.

But it also means that treating SpeechJudge-GRM as a standard **“single
utterance in, global MOS out”** predictor would be conceptually misleading
given the current data.

---

### (b) Why we do not present MOS-style numbers for GRM in this paper

In principle, one could try to construct MOS-like scores for a fixed text by
comparing a candidate against a curated set of same-text anchors and mapping
its relative position to a 1–5 scale. However:

- This would require **carefully designed anchor sets for each text** and
  additional assumptions about how to map relative preferences to an absolute
  scale.
- It still would **not match the common usage pattern of MOS predictors**
  (arbitrary text, single utterance input, no reference set), and we are wary
  of over-claiming MOS capabilities that our current data do not support.

Instead, we evaluate SpeechJudge-GRM **indirectly but more faithfully**:
in Section 5.4, when GRM is used as a reward for TTS post-training, the
resulting systems are **consistently preferred by human listeners** and
achieve higher **naturalness CMOS (N-CMOS)** than the base model and the DPO
baseline. This shows that GRM’s preference signal is *well aligned with human
perceived naturalness*, even though we do not convert it into per-utterance
MOS scores.

---

### (c) Future directions toward MOS-style modeling

We agree that bridging toward MOS-style evaluation is an exciting direction.
We now highlight in **Section 6 (Limitations and Future Work)** that:

- Extending SpeechJudge-Data with **cross-text comparisons** or a **small
  amount of direct MOS supervision** would make it possible to **calibrate the
  latent preference scores into globally comparable MOS-style values**; and  
- A dedicated MOS predictor could then be trained on top of SpeechJudge-Data,
  potentially using SpeechJudge-GRM as a strong initialization.

We assume that the reviewers' concern mainly arises because SpeechJudge-Eval shares the same construction pipeline as SpeechJudge-Data and is therefore **in-distribution by design**. However, we would like to clarify that this is intentional: it provides a controlled setting to compare different judges fairly on the distribution they are trained for. Moreover, as discussed before, we also introduce several **explicit OOD evaluations** in addition to reporting performance on
SpeechJudge-Eval:

  - best-of-N sample selection for **Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Talker)**,  
  - GRM-guided post-training of **Qwen2.5-0.5B-TTS** evaluated on external
    benchmarks (SeedTTS-Eval and Amphion-TTS-Eval), and  
  - the new challenging **human vs. SeedTTS clone** test.

In the revision, we will make this separation more explicit and move the new
human-vs-clone evaluation into the experimental narrative (Table 11 of Appendix G.1) to underline
that GRM is tested beyond its training distribution.

---

### (c) Generalization to out-of-distribution languages

Regarding **languages beyond Chinese/English/code-switching**: we fully agree
that evaluating on more languages (e.g., Japanese, Spanish, etc.) would be
valuable. At the same time, we would like to **clarify the intended scope**:

- SpeechJudge-Data and SpeechJudge-GRM are **explicitly focused** on
  **Chinese, English, and Chinese–English code-switching**.  
- Our annotators are **professional raters in China**, native in Mandarin with
  high but still L2 English proficiency (CET-6+).

We therefore **do not claim** that the current GRM is a universal,
language-agnostic naturalness judge. Extending SpeechJudge to new languages
would require:

- collecting **new preference annotations** from native or highly proficient
  listeners in those languages, and  
- ensuring **sufficient TTS diversity per language** to avoid overfitting to
  any single architecture.

We will state this clearly in **Section 6 (Limitations and Future Work)**: the
current release should be interpreted as a **TTS-focused naturalness judge for
Chinese, English, and their code-switching**, and extending it to broader
multilingual settings (with human recordings and more TTS families per
language) is an important direction for future work.

---

In summary, while SpeechJudge-Data is indeed synthetic-only and shares its
construction pipeline with SpeechJudge-Eval, we (i) design the dataset to
match the intended RLHF use case, (ii) diversify generators and styles to
reduce model-specific bias, and (iii) provide multiple OOD evaluations—
including on **real human speech vs. a strong commercial TTS**—which indicate
that SpeechJudge-GRM captures transferable naturalness cues rather than
memorizing artifacts of a single model family.

6. Quality control for expressive prompts and multilingual / code-switched scripts
```

*Comment:* How were the expressive prompts and multilingual scripts quality-controlled?

*Response:* We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. In our pipeline,
“expressive prompts” refer to the **speech references** \(a_{\text{ref}}\)
(emotional, accented, whisper, game-character voices), and “multilingual
scripts” refer to the **target texts** \(t\) (including code-switched
sentences). Both are carefully controlled at the **data-source level** and at
the **text-generation level**.

---

### (a) Expressive speech references

All expressive references in SpeechJudge-Data are **real human recordings**,
sourced from curated corpora that are designed for paralinguistic richness,
including:

- emotional corpora (e.g., ParaSpeechCaps–style resources),
- accented corpora (e.g., L2-Arctic, KeSpeech),
- an in-house whisper corpus, and
- character voices from the *Genshin Impact* game.

These corpora already provide **validated transcripts and style labels**
(emotion, accent, whisper, character). On top of that, when building
SpeechJudge-Data we:

- restrict segments to moderate duration (≈10–20 s) to avoid extremely short
  or unstable clips;
- discard segments with obvious ASR errors or strong non-speech noise
  (e.g., heavy background noise);
- manually spot-check samples from each expressive source to confirm that  
  (i) the intended style is clearly perceivable, and  
  (ii) the transcript matches the spoken content.

We will add a concise description of these steps in the revised paper.

summary.value: This work provides a human-annotated dataset for training automatic evaluators of TTS quality, and evaluates current automatic metrics against this dataset.  The paper also describes a new evaluator that is trained using this data by fine tuning with a standard evaluator followed by reinforcement learning on the dataset.  This new evaluator does improve other automatic metrics.

*Response:* We fully agree with the reviewer that, in an ideal setting,

particularly for high-quality TTS systems where only subtle cues distinguish
different outputs.

In the current work, however, all annotations were collected via a
**professional data-annotation company in China**, and the vast majority of
annotators are **native Mandarin speakers**:

- For **Mandarin** data, annotators are native speakers.  
- For **English and code-switched** data, we required annotators to have at
  least **CET-6–level English proficiency (or equivalent)**, and we applied
  per-annotator reliability screening (Appendix C.1).

As analyzed in **Appendix C.2 (Inter-Annotator Agreement)**:

- The overall agreement on SpeechJudge-Data (pref) is **69%**, comparable to
  standard RLHF corpora such as InstructGPT (72.6%) and ImageReward (65.3%).  
- Agreement is **higher on Chinese subsets** than on English / mixed subsets,
  which is consistent with the reviewer’s concern: subtle L2 and
  code-switching nuances are harder for non-native listeners.

In the revised paper, we now state this more explicitly in **Section 6
(“Limitations and Future Work”)**:

> our dataset primarily reflects the preferences of **Chinese and
> Chinese–English bilingual listeners**, not those of native English speakers.

We also highlight as future work:

- **Extending SpeechJudge-Data with native English raters** for the English
  subset, and  
- More broadly, **including annotators from multiple language communities**
  to better capture cross-cultural notions of “naturalness”.

We are also conducting a **small-scale validation study with native English
listeners on a subset of English pairs** as a follow-up sanity check; we will report the preliminary results in the next revised version of the work.

Overall, while the current annotator pool is constrained by practical
considerations, our analyses indicate that the English annotations are
sufficiently reliable to train and evaluate SpeechJudge-GRM, and we agree that
incorporating native English raters would further strengthen the dataset in
future iterations.
